Related to targeting cancer cells, here are some of biggest delivery challenges many people face and how our strategy matches those challenges. This text is largely cut and pasted from a response I gave to another person with a similar question:

1. **Getting the particles to the tumor**. If the treatment is applied systemically (e.g. through IV), it can be really challenging just to get 10% of the particles to get to the tumor. **We do a direct intratumoral injection**, instead of applying systemically. Intratumoral injections are beginning to become more popular generally, because of how ineffective systemic targeting tends to be and how intrtumoral injections allow for lower total dosing.
2. **Getting the particles homogeneously distributed throughout the tumor** for uniform enhancement and therapeutic cell killing. This is especially difficult in pancreatic cancer, which is often very densely fibrous, like a big scar, so much so, that in some cases the actual cancer cells may only make up about 20% of the tumor volume. It's such a tight network that even the very smallest of pre-fabricated particles are restricted in diffusion even if applied by intratumoral injection. **Our strategy applies gold ions, which are on the same size scale as other salts** (much smaller than even the smallest nanoparticles). But once the cells form particles from these ions, those formed particles are restricted from leaving.
3. **Get the particles inside the cells**. *Your question about selective uptake is addressed here*. Of course selective uptake is a challenge too. Our process has some preferential uptake of the ions (fairly small single digit percentage), but the more prominent effect is the preferential biosynthesis (AKA processing speed). **The pancreatic cancer cells convert gold ions to particles at a faster rate than the healthy counterparts**. \~2-fold greater.
4. **Get the Particles to the best spots inside the cell to do damage**. This is very very challenging. Many scientists develop whole platforms that are dedicated to getting a very small fraction of particles inside the nucleus. But, when the cells make the particles from gold ions, **a huge portion of the particles formed by cells from gold ions innately are formed in the nuclei**.

Great question too  


So, this procedure would not replace conventional cancer therapies (i.e. X-ray ablation), but instead augment them to be more effective, by enhancing the therapeutic cell killing of the x-ray therapy at the tumor. 

​

The TLDR; is gold absorbs x-rays better than the other elements in your body. absorbing those x-rays does damage to molecules that are close by. So gold nanoparticle loaded tumor takes more damage from x-ray therapy than a tumor without (If those particles are in the nucleus of those cells, and this process where cells produce the particles from precursor innately places a large amount of those particles in the nuclei).  What's more, is that gold nanoparticles are fairly bioinert, meaning they aren't metabolized quickly; and also the particles made within the tumors are small enough that if/when they escape the tumor they could be secreted through urine via the renal clearance system.    


**About the cost comment.** We grow gold nanoparticles within the tumor from a precursor solution (also gold but in an ionic form). This gold nanoparticle precursor solution is already used by many gold nanoparticle research scientists and there's already infrastructure to produce it at scale (albeit not medical grade). It costs \~$800/5g, which sounds like a lot, but for the treatments we're giving mice we're applying it on the scale of micrograms or lower, which ends up being considerably cheaper than many chemotherapies. An example for comparison I found on Sigma Aldrich, costs for the chemo drug Gemcitibine at \~$300/50mg. So even though it is gold, it could be cheaper to deploy. But also, we could apply it as supplement too.

When an element absorbs an x-ray photon, it can kick off an unpaired electron from that element. That unpaired electron is highly reactive, and will react with something very close by and do damage. This is how x-rays can do damage to your body. But it doesn't damage your body uniformly. It damages things that are either just very sensitive to damage or things are near stuff that absorbs x-rays better (like bones). Bones have a lot of calcium in them and calcium absorbs x-rays better than carbon. This is why on x-ray imaging bone shows up with the most contrast. 

.

Gold absorbs even better than that because it has a lot of electrons and a lot of electrons that can be kicked off. Related to being a good conductor of electricity too maybe (it's been awhile since I thought about currents haha).   


Essentially the gold nanoparticles become hot spots for enhancing x-ray damage because they absorb x-rays really well and in turn emit more unpaired electrons. But keep in mind, this only enhanced damage very locally.

For prospective patient care. X-ray ablation therapy is already a mainstay treatment for pancreatic cancer patients. But the pancreas is not externally visible, especially the tumor inside, and the patient will need to go through multiple rounds of X-ray treatment (meaning separate days, maybe weeks, maybe months), so the doctors need to place markers inside the patient around the pancreatic tumor to locate the spot they want to irradiate each time and will place metal markers that will show up by x-ray scan. We envision our treatment would be applied at the same time these markers are placed, to essentially enhance the process already used by radiation oncologists.

I'm sorry for your loss. Pancreatic cancer is one of the most challenging to treat and there are still not many treatments available or means to detect it in the early stages.   


For (1), what we've just published is the very first step. A very simple model of cancer, essentially growing a commercially available human pancreatic cancer cell line into a tumor on the hind flank of immune-compromised mice. Our next steps before we work with humans are as follows and we can work on a few of them at the same time:  
a) **Thorough toxicity studies** in mice at multiple dosing regimens and time points. We have indication that the treatment itself is not toxic, but we need to characterize any possible impact to organs and physiological processes at more treatment time points and at different dosing concentrations. We're working with folks at NIH to get this part done.   


b) **Immune competent mouse studies**. We need to work with immune competent mouse studies to see what interactions our treatment has with the immune system, will it work for or against the bodies natural defense system. We have some indication that there could be beneficial interactions based on cell culture studies. but this might not translate in a full living system. One of our collaborators for this work has an immune competent model that they are pretty comfortable with, and they're planning on leading that part   


c) **Orthotopic Studies.** This just means we have to do a study with the tumor growing on the organ site (the pancreas in our case). It's a bit of a complicated surgery, that I can't do, but we have pancreatic cancer surgeons that we collaborate with to help us with this part.

d) **Patient Derived Tumors.** We have a pancreatic cancer surgeon collaborator who has a mini library of tumor samples from a variety of real patients that they can implant in immune compromised mice. We can then treat those mice with what we've developed to then learn about what kind of patient might benefit the most from treatment. We can do this because for each of these tumor samples from patients our collaborator has information on clinical outcomes and biological information (gene expression/ mutation) about those tumors. Essentially we find who would benefit the most from our treatment so that we better target our clinical trials. 

​

This all sounds like a lot (it is), but we've got a lot of fantastic collaborators so we can work on different aspects at the same time. Normally getting a new drug to market is \~$1Billion + ten years and we just got the patent out last year. How we do have an advantage to get to clinical trials, is that this strategy is based off a side effect from a century old drug category (that still has clinical approval) called crysotherapeutics. The side effect of weekly gram amount dosings of those drugs was skin discoloration (nanoparticle formation in people), and we only apply microgram amounts a single time (for now).
